author: Robert Booth UK technology editor
description:
Nobel winner who devised concept of neural network warns AI could be near to triggering major incident such as power or banking shutdown

One of the “godfathers of AI”, Geoffrey Hinton, has said it could turn out that humans would have been better off never developing the technology as he warned it could trigger a large-scale incident this year or next such as a temporary blackout of financial or power systems.

The Nobel prize-winning computer scientist told the Guardian he is not a “doomer” about the technology that is underpinned by his groundbreaking research into artificial neural networks and believes AI has the potential to lead to a “wonderful future” but he said “it might be that we would have been better off never developing it”.

National Transportation Safety Board says discovery of parts confirms plane was breaking apart before it crashed

National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) member Tom Chapman said during a news conference on Tuesday that the discovery of tail parts broken into three pieces confirms the plane was breaking apart before it hit the ground.

You have to try your best, keep putting on performances.”

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Readers respond to an article by Andy Burnham in which he says that people today can’t be held personally liable for the country’s historical wrongs

In his opinion piece (30 October), Andy Burnham argues that British people today cannot be held liable for historical wrongs “in which they played no personal part”. On one level, he is right. But he confuses two very different things: personal liability and the continuing responsibility of the state.

When slavery was abolished in the British empire in 1833, the government borrowed £20m – an extraordinary sum then – to compensate enslavers for the loss of their supposed property. Some 40,000 claims were made. The British taxpayer carried the cost, and the resulting public debt was not finally cleared until 2015.
title: Britain must have the courage to face its legacy of slavery | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Dave Hunter suggests requiring the event to be online and inviting Hope Not Hate to speak on another occasion

The question of whether Oriel College, Oxford, should host Nathan Cofnas highlights the double bind for educational institutions created by the freedom of speech legislation from 2023: bad law, designed to fix a non-problem relating to “no platforming” (Oriel College urged to cancel student group’s event with Jason Arday accuser, 27 October).

However, such institutions have options. Oriel could require the event to be online, and solely for the members of the relevant society. This could help to mitigate security risks and the impact on students outside that society.
title: How Oxford University’s Oriel College should handle Nathan Cofnas event | Letter

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Nick Lowe on the director’s unusual collaboration with the singer-songwriter Dory Previn

Peter Medak’s long career was a book of many chapters (Peter Medak, veteran director of The Krays and The Changeling, dies aged 88, 28 October), but one of the more unusual ones was his collaboration with the singer-songwriter Dory Previn, with whom he developed several projects during his short-lived first Hollywood phase after The Ruling Class and A Day in the Death of Joe Egg had made him hot property.

Previn’s semi-autobiographical screenplay, The Third Girl from the Left, became Medak’s first US feature, a 1973 TV movie – though on this occasion his Hollywood career failed to ignite and he served out the rest of the 70s back in the UK. But he retained a great fondness for D
title: Peter Medak’s work with Dory Previn was one of his career’s more unusual chapters | Letter

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Dr Susannah O’Hanlon responds to an article that claimed in-person dog training can cost £150 an hour

Your article (Bone of contention: why dog trainers are at war, 28 October) says “in-person training can cost £150 an hour”. I do wonder where you got that figure from. I am a postgraduate-qualified clinical animal behaviourist and an accredited dog trainer with the Professional Association of Canine Trainers, with more than 16 years’ experience, and I charge £60 an hour for in-person training in affluent Cambridge. Delighted to hear I can double my prices.

I don’t endorse the use of prong, shock or spray collars as I work under the assumption that most people, like me, love their dogs and don’t want to subject them to unpleasant startles, pain or fear. Treats are part of what we use, but relationships are built on so much more than
title: A barking-mad fee to train your dog | Letters

author: Sarah Butler
description:
Budget retailer and 12,000 jobs at risk after US owner fails to accept buyout offers

MPs have called on the government to protect Poundland and other high street stores from “predatory capitalism” and asset-stripping.

The fate of the retail chain and its 12,000 staff remains uncertain after it filed a notice of intention to appoint administrators at the high court last Thursday.

author: John Crace
description:
Launching a defence plan on a rusty sloop, and dogged by a UK Iron Dome that never was, the Tory leader has forgotten her party’s 14 years in power

HMS Wellington. A decommissioned Grimsby-class sloop from the second world war. A warship that has been moored on the Thames, going nowhere for the best part of 80 years. Today’s venue for the leader of the opposition to explain why the Conservative party hollowed out defence spending throughout their time in office. Sorry. Scrub that. To welcome in a brave new world order. Come aboard the good ship Badenoch. There are times when you wonder if the Tory media team have been infiltrated by Labour HQ. Still, we might as well enjoy it while we can.

After a brief introduction from the loyal but dim Lieutenant “Steady as she goes, chaps and chapesses” James Cartlidge, who – for reasons not even he fully understands – is the shadow defence secretary, Kaptain Kemi appeared to take over the helm. “Why have I brought you here?” she be
title: All aboard with Kaptain Kemi, lost at sea on the good ship amnesia

author: Guardian community team
description:
Whether you are a customer who has used AI to show a baker your dream cake, or a baker who has to up their game - or turn down – orders based on AI inspo, we want to hear from you

AI tools like Claude and ChatGPT are now widely used – including for creative inspiration. We are keen to hear from people on what happens when AI meets a physical art: baking.

Whether you are a customer who has used AI to show a baker your dream cake, or a baker who has to up their game - or turn down – orders based on AI inspo, we want to hear from you. Has AI led to extraordinary creations, or almighty disasters? Tell us all about it below.

description:
Retailer acquires robot-assisted warehouse and intends to have UK service up and running before end of 2027

Primark is to begin making home deliveries by the end of next year as it aims to win new shoppers after a slide in profits.

author: Rachel Hall
description:
Kellogg’s substitutes ingredient with rice flour, as climate crisis affects availability of some grains

They will snap and they will crackle, but they may no longer pop, as Kellogg’s has removed rice from its Rice Krispies and Coco Pops cereals due to “changing weather conditions”.

Rice Krispies has been reformulated to use rice flour instead of rice, while Coco Pops now contain a blend of rice flour and corn flour instead of rice in order to maintain consistent quality. Kelloggs’ said the shift reflected how the climate crisis had affected the quality and availability of some rice and grains used in its most popular cereals.

Continue reading...

author: Caroline Voaden
description:
His boorish behaviour towards me typifies the politics of Reform UK: this is a party full of disdain for parliament, its people and its traditions

I got an unexpected message last week from a former colleague whom I haven’t heard from in 20 years. I was all over her TikTok, she said, so she reached out to say hi. Such was the furore caused by Nigel Farage bizarrely raising an incident that took place in the House of Commons nearly six months ago that I suddenly found myself trending on social media. That had not been on my bingo card for budget week.

I was at home, having just got back from London, when I received a message telling me that Farage had referenced “the incident”. I looked at the footage of his press conference and was completely dumbfounded. Because this “phy

author: Guardian community team
description:
With household budgets under pressure due to rising costs, we want to hear if you are doing anything differently this festive season

With just over seven weeks until Christmas, and the cost of living continuing to put pressure on household budgets, are you planning to celebrate differently this year to save money or reduce waste?

Perhaps you’re hosting a smaller gathering, buying secondhand gifts, organising a family Secret Santa or agreeing not to exchange presents between adults. Maybe you’re focusing more on spending time together and sharing experiences rather than exchanging gifts or finding other ways to make Christmas less wasteful.

author: David Jays
description:
To be with the woman he loved, Max Olesker had to convert to Orthodox Judaism – which required an unwelcome operation. He relives a painful and sometimes infuriating journey

When Max met Eliana at the Edinburgh fringe, the romcom vibes were strong. Shots, songs, falling headlong in love. Less vibey was the conversion Max Olesker had to navigate to marry his Orthodox Jewish beloved. The comedian had always thought of himself as Jewish – when his parents married, his mum converted to a less rigorous branch of Judaism. But to the Beth Din, the rabbinical court, that didn’t count. To be with the woman he loved, Max would have to go all in – including undergoing an unwelcome adult circumcision.

We’re chatting at a kosher restaurant in central London. Olesker, 38, pulls out a camera, snapping his hefty salt beef on rye from several angles (“I’m trying to learn a skill”). As on stage, he’s an engaging presence: bright eyes, smart, ribbed knitwear, unwaveringly polite. He would
title: My fiancee, my foreskin and me: the comic who turned adult circumcision into a jaw-dropping show

author: Miatta Mbriwa
description:
Garden Climate Assessment Tool will allow users to predict a plant’s response to the projected climate in a given location

“In the 20th century, we could pretty much grow the same things with confidence, we could learn from previous generations,” said Prof Sam Brockington, a curator at Cambridge University Botanic Garden.

“But now we’re moving into climate scenarios that we just don’t have the traditions to understand fully.”

Continue reading...
title: New tool will help gardeners move away from thirsty English classics to drought-resistant plants

author: Leslie Felperin
description:
Mucus, alien gristle, a tentacle-bearing penis and, of course, the pregnancy of the title are all borne with deadpan calmness in this underplayed comedy

In this amusingly silly exercise in gross-out body horror and bathos from New Zealand, thirtysomething underachiever Mary (Hannah Lynch) finds herself unexpectedly pregnant after shy neighbour Boo (Arlo Green) ejaculates on her in the communal laundry room with his tentacle-bearing alien penis (hence the self-explanatory title). We never quite find out why Boo has such outre sex organs, but nothing here should be overthought since it is all about setting up moments where the New Zealand cast react with deadpan calmness (or at best mild annoyance) to the most bizarre circumstances, as if it’s all just another Tuesday on South Island.

Fortunately, the cast is well up for serving this sort of underplayed comedy, especially supporting players Yvette Parsons and Jackie van Beek, as Mary and Arlo’s single mums Cynthia and Ann
title: Mum, I’m Alien Pregnant review – slime and silliness in amusing New Zealand comedy horror

author: Claudia Efemini
description:
The Super Falcons won’t be at the World Cup and with the prize money going up, they risk being left even further behind

It was a historic result in Casablanca – but not in a good way. Nigeria’s 2-1 defeat against South Africa in a playoff in August meant that the Super Falcons are missing out on the World Cup for the first time. It is a crushing blow for the most decorated national side in Africa across both men and women, one that has won no fewer than 10 Wafcon titles.

The journalist and lecturer Dr Victor Ademola was in Morocco the day of the defeat. “It was a very difficult evening,” he says. “Some players were visibly emotional while others appeared to be processing what had just happened. I saw players crying as they got on to the team bus while some sat alone or remained on their phones, looking very sad.”
title: ‘An absolute afterthought’: the story of the Nigeria women’s team’s fall from grace

Though a lot of people are about to win – or lose – a lot of money, it’s hard to imagine any wagers as consequential as the election bet that birthed a sporting craze spearheaded by a chancer who walked and talked his way into becoming one of the greatest athletic stars of the 19th century.

author: Rebecca Nicholson
description:
The author gets a backstage pass to the personal life of the world’s most famous woman – but what do we really learn?

The magazine writer Jonathan Van Meter profiles very famous people for extremely glossy publications. He was responsible for the notorious 1990 interview in which supermodel Linda Evangelista said she wouldn’t wake up for less than $10,000 a day, and in recent years, he has interviewed Taylor Swift, Michelle Obama and Lady Gaga for American Vogue. In 2019, he wrote a cover story, also for Vogue, on Kim Kardashian, the reality TV star turned business­woman turned criminal justice activist, and one of the most famous women in the world. In the lengthy acknowledgments to this book, he describes receiving a phonecall from her after the piece had been published. “There’s no better feeling in the world than when someone gets you,” she told him. He replied by telling her that he was going to write a book about her, “whether you like it or not!”

S
title: Citizen Kim by Jonathan Van Meter review – Kardashian under the microscope

Control of the Senate and House of Representatives, both currently held by the Republicans, is at stake

author: Yagnishsing Dawoor
description:
This propulsive, globe-trotting tale brilliantly skewers the corruption and corporatisation of higher education

It’s no secret that academia is on the blink; Canadian author Randy Boyagoda’s new novel, which is equal parts satire, dystopia and exposé, tells the story of all that’s wrong, glitchy and broken. Set across Sri Lanka, the United States and Italy, it centres on a cast of students, parents and professors, and their dealings with a common antagonist: the university.

The first character we meet is Sri Lankan teen Devi, who is set on obtaining offers from “Ochpys” – her acronym for Oxford, Cambridge, Harvard, Princeton, Yale and Stanford. To help her realise her dream, Devi’s family of modest means – her mother, father, maternal grandmother and two brothers – hire themselves out as mourners at the funerals of the wealthy. Most of this money goes towards paying Johannes, her tutor on WhatsApp who, unbeknown to Devi, is a hard-up Indian student at Arcadia Tech, an
title: Lords of Serendipity by Randy Boyagoda review – a campus satire for this moment of crisis

author: Catherine Bray
description:
Two outsider students at a super-strict high school find they are definitely not with the programme in Yûta Shimotsu’s body-bending sci-fi scarer

Here is an intermittently amusing Japanese social satire about conformity directed by Yûta Shimotsu; it has flashes of brilliance but lacks the kind of engaging characters that could have taken it to the next level. Ai (Anna Yamada) is an unpopular pupil who has always tried to fit in, and Yu (Yuzu Aoki) is a transfer student who more deliberately resists the demands of peer pressure. Their high school is super-strict at a baseline level – and when things start to degenerate, with students forming themselves into human pyramids and turning into mindless drones, it becomes clear something extremely peculiar is at work.

Fans of The Faculty, Robert Rodriguez and Kevin Williamson’s 1998 high-school riff on Invasion of the Body Snatchers, might be pricking up their ears at this point, but New Group is a less straightforward narrati
title: New Group review – schoolkids build human pyramids in bizarre Japanese horror-satire on conformity

author: Sarah Butler
description:
Steve Smith calls on owners to accept proposed buyout as 12,000 staff face uncertain future in run-up to Christmas

The founder of Poundland has warned that staff at the retailer could be out of work for “years” if it collapses, as he called on the owners of the troubled chain to accept a proposed buyout deal.

Steve Smith, who set up the firm with a store in Burton upon Trent in 1990, said: “Once these jobs are lost, they are lost” from Britain’s struggling high streets. His warning comes as the chain’s 12,000 employees face uncertainty over their future in the run-up to Christmas.

Continue reading...
title: Poundland staff could be out of work for years if retailer collapses, founder says

author: Chris Cotonou
description:
Just an hour from London, this idyllic area, beloved by painters and poets, is brimming with history, beautiful walks and fab places to eat and drink

In the 1820s, a young painter left London to live in Shoreham in the west of Kent. In his waterside cottage, Samuel Palmer – remembered now as a key figure of British Romanticism – depicted moonlit cornfields, apple trees bowed under fruit and hills swollen with light. He dubbed the area his Valley of Vision. Two centuries on, Palmer’s own vision of Shoreham – and the surrounding Darent Valley – as a demi-paradise isn’t too far from the canvas.

I’ve lived in the area for five years and can’t quite believe how few people come to Shoreham. It feels like a secret yet is less than an hour from London by train. The village itself sits on the River Darent, remarked on by Edmund Spenser in his poem The Faerie Queene for its gentleness and clear water: “The still Darent, in whose waters cleane, ten thousand fishes play and decke h
title: A perfect weekend in the Darent valley, Kent: a ‘demi-paradise’ of art, lavender fields and great pubs

description:
Nicolas Rachline’s stunning book Elsebound is full of painterly photographs inspired by Edward Hopper and Blade Runner. He explains his uniquely haunting style

author: Rosie Peters-McDonald
description:
Hope Haven in Whitehaven is one of six trial open-access, 24/7 schemes in England offering preventive care

The night Tamara first walked through the doors of Hope Haven, a new community mental health hub in the heart of Whitehaven, she was afraid. “Terrified, actually,” she says. “Like, my life was falling apart. I didn’t know how to stop it from hurting.”

The 22-year-old, who works in children’s transport, had been in and out of therapy and counselling since she was 14, after being abused by an acquaintance as a child. After a lengthy legal process her abuser was sentenced, but the “mental challenge” of dealing with what had happened to her was not over.

Continue reading...
title: ‘This is direct’: positive early feedback from pilot community mental health hub in Cumbria

author: Peter Walker Senior political correspondent
description:
Exclusive: Members may be vetted before getting security passes for parliament, and receive anti-harassment training

MPs and others working in parliament could be required to take a criminal record check before being given a security pass, and receive anti-harassment training under a pioneering scheme to root out violence against women.

The UK parliament will on Tuesday become the first legislature in the world to receive what is known as White Ribbon accreditation, a commitment to culture change which originated in Canada.

Continue reading...
title: UK MPs could undergo criminal record checks to stop violence against women

author: Amy Fleming
description:
Our house was a mouse-free zone until our new kittens began venturing into the nearby woods in search of prey and playthings

This is a cat-and-mouse story in which the cats are the real pests. My old house, despite being next to rodent-filled woods, was blissfully mouse-free … until, during lockdown, we got two kittens, Mimi and Ruben. As soon as their fine motor skills were sufficiently sharpened, they started hunting. Thankfully, they weren’t into birds, but wood mice became their specialism. I suppose the dearth of mice indoors meant they had to catch them outside. The tabby twins would then bring their prey back to their lair (our house) and release them, still miraculously alive. Perhaps they thought mice would make fun pets.

You would know they had brought in a mouse when they sat guarding sections of ill-fitting skirting or gaps under cupboard doors, uttering odd “prittering” sounds. Cue us humans moving furniture and dashing about, getting down on our hands and
title: The pest I’ll never forget: the cats who filled our house with live mice

author: Phil Harrison, Ali Catterall and Simon Wardell
description:
A nurse with a drug habit is tempted by a gangster’s money in Tall Tales and Murder. Plus: an inside look at Burnham’s first 100 days. Here’s what to watch this evening

10.40pm, BBC One
This breezy Irish crime caper is directed by Chris Addison and stars the excellent Ella Lily Hyland as Bridget, a kindly nurse with a secret drug habit, a taste for folk horror stories and a willingness to dispatch suffering patients. When patient Grinner (Aidan Gillen) wakes from a coma and reveals himself to be a gangster with a hoard of buried treasure, Bridget spies an opportunity. Twisty fun with an edge of danger. Phil Harrison

author: Mark Cocker
description:
Hortobágy, Hungary: Their sheer size is striking enough, but the noise is something else, especially when they gather in huge migratory flocks

With a standing height of 1.4 metres, common cranes are Europe’s tallest birds and at this famous national park they collect in astonishing numbers as they migrate.

The autumn count is 180,000, although the only accessible spot to see them supports a sub-roost of 50,000. Each bird has a wingspan of 2 metres and the flight is slow and rhythmically precise. The visual effect of any large airborne congregation is at the scale of a whole landscape and its skies above.

Continue reading...
title: Country diary: The sound of thousands of cranes is truly oceanic | Mark Cocker

author: Agencies
description:
• Star defensive lineman has one sack, six tackles

  • D’Andre Swift rushes for three touchdowns

  • Seattle have lost three of their last four games

Caleb Williams threw a touchdown pass on the opening drive and Jeffery Simmons delivered just what Chicago needed on defense as the Bears beat the host Seattle Seahawks 34-17 on Monday night.

Williams was extremely efficient for the Bears (6-2) against one of the NFL’s stingiest defenses, committing no turnovers, taking just one sack and throwing for 247 yards while completing 71% of his passes.

Continue reading...

• Jockey Ethan Brown salutes after chasing down Royal Supremacy

  • Winning trainer Ciaron Maher fills top three places at Flemington

Point of Law justified his favouritism at the 2026 Melbourne Cup after the three-year-old stallion that was owned by King Charles until earlier this year reeled in Royal Supremacy in a thrilling feature race at Flemington Racecourse.

Jockey Ethan Brown guided the Ciaron Maher-trained horse to victory in the $10m race after Royal Supremacy – another in Maher’s stable – had led by about 20 lengths at one point.

author: Jonathan Yerushalmy
description:
Iranian state media reported the sound of explosions on the island in the strait of Hormuz, coming on the eve of crucial US midterms

The ⁠US launched limited strikes on ​Iran’s Qeshm Island late on Monday, ⁠according to reports in US media, hours after US vice-president JD Vance said he was optimistic diplomatic efforts to end the war were moving in the right direction.

The strikes were reported as being “defensive”, and not thought to be a signal of a return to full hostilities, but came on the eve of crucial midterm elections in which Donald Trump’s Republican party is expected to be punished by voters for the cascading effect the war has had on the US cost of living.

Continue reading...
title: US reportedly strikes Iran’s Qeshm Island as Vance voices optimism about a deal
